submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole fires when the clause under way predicates something about a person: activation climbs through the first few tokens of the predicate (the copula or auxiliary - is, was, are, am, have, can - a predicate adverb such as 'also', 'not', 'mainly', or a possessive/relative pronoun that refers back to the person: his, who, or its for an organisation) whenever the clause's subject denotes a human being (a name, he/she/I/you, a human noun phrase) or a body of people (an organisation, committee, institution, family). It falls to near zero when the identical predicate is applied to an inanimate or abstract subject ('the building', 'the machine', 'the protein', 'it') - the same surface token ('also', 'very', 'was') is typically 2-4x weaker, so the personhood of the subject, not the token identity, sets the strength.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Only three families remained in the valley through the winter of the siege. They shared the last of the flour, melted snow for water, and carried the dead up to the orchard behind the chapel. When the roads reopened in spring, traders brought salt, needles and news from the coast, and for a few weeks the square filled with strangers. Most of the survivors left before the next harvest. The Havel family stayed, rebuilt the mill wheel, and planted two rows of plum trees along the eastern wall. Their daughter Anna kept the parish ledger, recording every birth, marriage and funeral in a careful hand. Travellers who lost their way learned to knock at her door, and she would give them bread, a bed for the night, or directions to the ford. Anna taught the children of the village in the room above the stable, and she refused payment from families who had lost their harvest. She argued with the priest about the school, wrote letters for neighbours who could not write, and kept a list of every child who came to her door. Her son Josef took over the mill and enlarged the granary; his wife Barbora raised bees and sold honey at the market in the next town. Anna's brother Matej learned the cooper's trade and returned with a cart of barrels, which he repaired for farmers across the district. He never married, and he spent his evenings carving small wooden birds for the children who came to the workshop. When the floods came in 1897, he rowed families from the lower houses to the church hill and back until the water fell. The parish council gave him a silver cup, and he kept it on the shelf beside the birds. Josef served on the parish council for twelve years and pressed for a bridge over the ford, though the county delayed the work until after his death. The railway reached the district in 1904, and the traffic on the old road dwindled. Josef sold the mill to a cooperative, and the family moved into the house beside the chapel. Anna's granddaughter, my grandmother, kept the ledger locked in a wooden chest and read from it aloud on winter evenings. In the parish record, beside the list of teachers, my grandmother is also remembered for teaching half the village to read.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long narrative about people with the claimed person-predicate 'my grandmother is also remembered' deep near the end, testing the feature in a novel far-position context.
